schema.description: UHN ICF Automation Pipeline — canonical template registry.

symbol_guide.{{placeholder}}: REQUIRED substitution. Replace the entire {{...}} token with study-specific information extracted from the protocol.
symbol_guide.{{option1/option2}}: CHOOSE ONE. Pick the applicable option from the slash-separated list inside the braces (e.g., {{will/may}}, {{you/they}}, {{study/clinical trial}}).
symbol_guide.<Condition label>: CONDITIONAL BLOCK (single angle brackets). Include the text that follows this marker only if the stated condition applies to the study. Typically used for a single-paragraph or single-sentence addition (e.g., <If time permits>, <For single-blind studies>).
symbol_guide.<<Condition block>>: CONDITIONAL BLOCK (double angle brackets). Same meaning as <...> but conventionally marks a larger or more distinct scenario block, often with mutually exclusive alternatives (e.g., <<For single arm studies>>, <<If data sent outside Canada>>). Treat identically to <...> for extraction purposes.
symbol_guide.OR (standalone line): ALTERNATIVE. Choose exactly one of the blocks immediately above or below this marker — do not include both.
symbol_guide.• or - (list markers): BULLET POINT. Both markers are used interchangeably as list items.

field_guide.heading: UPPERCASE section heading as it appears in the ICF template.
field_guide.sub_section: Sub-section name, or null if none.
field_guide.required: true = must be included; false = include only if relevant to this study.
field_guide.complexity: Classification tags indicating extraction difficulty and protocol availability. Drives the RLM iteration budget and availability flags.
field_guide.is_in_protocol: true if the information is expected to be findable in the study protocol.
field_guide.partially_in_protocol: true if only some fields can be extracted from the protocol; the rest require manual entry by the study team.
field_guide.is_standard_text: true if required_text is boilerplate that can be used verbatim — no extraction needed.
field_guide.instructions: Author-facing directions for writing this ICF section. Not participant-facing. Used to guide LLM extraction.
field_guide.required_text: Mandated ICF wording. Contains {{placeholders}} to be filled in. Empty string if the section uses suggested_text only.
field_guide.suggested_text: Sample ICF language to use as a starting point. Contains <conditions>, <<block conditions>>, {{placeholders}}, and OR alternatives. Not required wording — adapt to the study.
field_guide.suggested_text_format: 'text' (default) or 'html' — set to 'html' and use an HTML string in suggested_text when table content is needed (e.g., section 13.6).
field_guide.adaptation_notes: Runtime-only field. Set by the dynamic adaptation pass to inject study-specific context into extraction prompts. Always null in the base registry; never serialised back to this file.

Below is a summary of information about the study.  There is more information in the document called an "informed consent form" that follows this summary.  Please read the informed consent form.   The research team will also talk to you about the study and you can ask any questions you may have.

Participation in research is voluntary.  It is your choice whether you take part in this clinical trial.

sections.heading: Summary of Informed Consent Form
sections.instructions:
Briefly describe the study design, intervention(s), and highlight key study procedures and, if applicable, outline procedures that may be lengthy/burdensome to participants.

Fill the placeholders in the required text: name the interventional group(s); briefly describe the key procedures (e.g., the frequency of study visits and what happens at them); and, if applicable, describe any lengthy or burdensome procedures and how much extra time they take. The 'If applicable:' clause about lengthy/burdensome procedures should be included only when such procedures exist. You are allowed to edit the required text a bit at the end just to make the paragraph coherent and in plain grade 8 correct language

sections.heading: Summary of Informed Consent Form
sections.instructions:
Describe the most important risks. Consider those most probable and/or of highest magnitude of harm. This summary should NOT include the full list of risks.

For the 'most likely' risks: include the risks participants are most likely to experience, specified in lay language with their expected frequency. Provide one bullet per risk.

For the 'most serious' risks: include this part only if applicable. For the purposes of this summary, serious risks are considered those that may result in death, hospitalization, or are permanent. Specify each in lay language with expected frequency, one bullet per risk.

sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
complexity: Not in protocol - requires manual entry
sections.instructions:
STUDY TYPE: Determine whether this is a 'study' or a 'clinical trial' (a type of study that involves research) for the {{study/clinical trial (a type of study that involves research)}} placeholder. Do not infer that a study is a clinical trial based on study design characteristics (e.g., randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled, prospective, controlled trial, intervention arms). Only classify as a clinical trial when the protocol explicitly states that the study is a clinical trial, or clearly identifies itself as a Phase I, Phase II, Phase III, or Phase IV clinical trial. Otherwise use 'study'.

{{main features of population}}: Describe only the direct circumstance that makes the individual eligible for this study. Focus on the specific condition, diagnosis, treatment, procedure, or clinical situation that is relevant to study participation (e.g., 'you have been diagnosed with [condition]', 'you are scheduled for [procedure]', 'you are a healthy adult volunteer'). Do not explain the full eligibility criteria, demographic requirements (e.g., age ranges), symptoms, underlying disease details, or provide descriptions of medical procedures unless they are necessary to understand why the person is being approached for the study.

DECISION TIMEFRAME (choose exactly one — these are mutually exclusive):
  Option A (default): 'Please take your time in making your decision.' — use when no strict enrollment window applies.
  Option B: 'The study staff will tell you about the study timelines for making your decision.' — use ONLY when participants must start intervention within a specific timeframe due to best practices for the participant population/disease.

{{Specify other potential participant concerns}}: Specify any other areas where participants might be concerned about a potential penalty or discrimination (e.g., 'The decision will not affect your employment'). Omit if no such concerns apply.

{{impact on future healthcare options}}: If the study may affect future healthcare options, include the optional sentence beginning 'However; it may affect your future health care options…'. This typically applies to studies involving investigational therapies that may exclude participants from future treatment lines.
sections.required_text:
You are being invited to participate in a research {{study/clinical trial (a type of study that involves research)}}. You are invited to participate in this study because you {{main features of population}}. This consent form provides you with information to help you make an informed choice. Please read this document carefully and ask any questions you may have. All your questions should be answered to your satisfaction before you decide whether to participate in this research study. You may find it helpful to discuss it with your friends and family.

<If time permits — CHOOSE ONE of the following two options, do not include both>:
Please take your time in making your decision.
OR
<For clinical trials where participants must start intervention within a specific timeframe due to best practices for the participant population/disease>
The study staff will tell you about the study timelines for making your decision.

Taking part in this study is voluntary. You have the option to not participate at all or you may choose to leave the study at any time. Whatever you choose, it will not affect the usual medical care that you receive outside the study. <If the study may affect future healthcare options, include:> However; it may affect your future health care options. This will be discussed with you. If you have any questions about this, you can ask the study team. {{Specify other potential participant concerns, such as penalties, discrimination, or impact on employment — omit if none apply}}

sections.heading: IS THERE A CONFLICT OF INTEREST?
complexity: Not in protocol - requires manual entry
sections.instructions:
ALWAYS include this section — every ICF must declare conflicts of interest (or state there are none).

Describe any conflict of interest that exists or may appear to exist for any investigator, study staff member, or member of their immediate family. A conflict of interest exists if there is a potential personal benefit — including academic achievement, publication credit, or presentation of results. Common examples include: speaker's fees, travel assistance, consultant fees, honoraria, gifts, and intellectual property rights (patents).

A complete declaration must include:
1. The IDENTITY of the person with the conflict of interest
2. The TYPE of incentive or inducement
3. The SOURCE of the benefit

SELECT the most appropriate option from the suggested_text below:
- Option 1: Investigator receives personal financial payment from an external source
- Option 2: The institution/hospital receives financial payment (indirect conflict)
- Option 3: Sponsor reimburses hospital/researcher for study costs (sponsored studies — most common)
- Option 4: Researchers have a general interest in completing the study (internally funded studies — minimal conflict)

Note: This section is marked 'Not in protocol' because specific financial relationships between investigators and sponsors are typically not documented in the clinical protocol itself. The study team must provide this information directly.
sections.suggested_text:
<for Option 1, personal payment to investigator, use the following>
The {{study doctor/researcher}}, {{insert name}}, is receiving personal financial payment from {{identify source of funds}} for {{include reason for payment}}. You may request details about this payment.
OR
<for option 2, the institution/hospital receiving financial payment, use the following>
The {{insert recipient of funding}} is receiving financial payment from the {{Sponsor/Funder}} to cover the cost of conducting this study.
OR
<For Option 3, sponsored studies, use the following>
{{Insert name of company}}, the sponsor of this study, will reimburse the hospital and researcher for the costs of doing this study. All of these people have an interest in completing this study. Their interests should not influence your decision to participate in this study.
OR
<For option 4, internally funded studies, use the following>
Researchers have an interest in completing this study. Their interests should not influence your decision to participate in this study.

sections.heading: WHAT IS THE BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR THIS STUDY?
complexity: Not in protocol - requires manual entry
sections.instructions:
PURPOSE OF THIS SECTION: Explain the context and scientific rationale for the study. Begin by describing the reason why the research question is being studied. Focus on the research question rather than study procedures. Do not assume that a drug, procedure, surgery, or treatment mentioned in the protocol is the focus of the research unless it is the subject of the research question. Protocols frequently mention background therapies, standard-of-care agents, and concomitant procedures that are not what the study is testing.

Briefly explain the current standard of care, standard treatment, or current approach, clearly distinguishing it from the study intervention. Describe the reason the study is being conducted, focusing on what researchers are trying to better understand or evaluate. Do not imply that current treatments are inadequate or that the study intervention may be superior, safer, more effective, or otherwise beneficial. Explain only to the extent necessary to understand why the research is needed. Conclude with what the study is trying to learn or address.

Use neutral, objective, non-coercive language throughout. Ensure this section is written in plain lay language, explaining information in a manner that supports understanding for the research participant. When including statistics or numbers, avoid vague terms such as "a few," "some," or "many" unless explicitly defined in the source material.

When the study involves an investigational drug, device, or novel intervention, indicate whether it has previously been tested in humans. If no prior human studies have been conducted, clearly state that the study is first-in-human.

Keep this section concise, generally up to 8-10 sentences.

CONTENT ORDER: Always present the background information (condition, standard of care, rationale for the study) BEFORE any Health Canada regulatory statement.

HEALTH CANADA OVERSIGHT: Determine from the protocol whether the study involves a drug, device, or natural health product regulated by Health Canada (i.e., the study has an IND, IDE, or similar regulatory filing with Health Canada).
  - If YES: include the required_text block, choosing exactly ONE of the two options.
      Option 1 — the product IS approved in Canada but is being used outside its approved parameters (new indication, or a different dose/schedule).
      Option 2 — the product is NOT yet approved anywhere in Canada.
  - If NO (e.g., observational study, an approved device used within its approved parameters, or an investigator-initiated non-drug study): OMIT the required_text block entirely and produce the section from suggested_text only.
sections.required_text:
<<Include ONLY for studies under Health Canada oversight — choose exactly ONE of the two options below>>

<<Option 1: Product/agent/device IS approved in Canada but used outside approved parameters (e.g., approved for a different condition, or at a different dose/schedule)>>
{{Insert name(s) of product/agent/device}} is approved in Canada to treat {{specify condition/disease}}. Health Canada, the regulatory body that oversees the use of {{natural health products/drugs/devices}} in Canada, has not approved the sale or use of {{insert name(s) of product/agent/device}} for {{specify change from approved parameters}}. Health Canada has allowed {{insert name(s) of product/agent/device}} to be used in this study.

<<Option 2: Product/agent/device is NOT approved by Health Canada at all>>
Health Canada, the regulatory body that oversees the use of {{natural health products/drugs/devices}} in Canada, has not approved the sale or use of {{insert name(s) of product/agent/device}}. Health Canada has allowed {{insert name(s) of product/agent/device}} to be used in this study.
sections.suggested_text:
The standard or usual treatment for {{specify condition}} is {{describe the standard treatment}}.

<<Include and modify the following section to align with the study>>
{{Insert name(s) of product/agent/device}} is a {{describe whether it is a natural health product/drug/device, and whether it is new or existing}} for {{specify condition}}. 

<<Include and modify if there are any earlier laboratory tests related to this natural health product/drug/device>>
Laboratory tests show that it may {{explain laboratory results in lay terminology}}.

<<Include the following if relevant>>
 It has been studied in a few people and seems promising but it is not clear if it can offer better results than standard treatment.

<<Include the following if relevant>>

sections.heading: WHY IS THIS STUDY BEING DONE?
sections.instructions:
PURPOSE OF THIS SECTION: Explain the specific question(s) this study is designed to answer and why the research is being conducted. Identify information from the study's primary objective, research question, study aim, and/or hypothesis, and focus on what the researchers are trying to determine rather than how the study is conducted (procedures are covered in the study procedures section). Start with the primary objective. If any additional objectives are identified in the protocol, briefly summarize them after the primary objective. Preserve key study-specific details needed to understand the study purpose. Do not assume that a drug, device, procedure, treatment, participant population, biological sample, organ, or other element mentioned in the protocol is the focus of the study unless identified as an objective. Use neutral, objective language and describe only what the researchers are investigating. Do not use terms such as "success," "better," "improves outcomes," "safer," or similar language that suggests benefit, effectiveness, superiority, or a favorable outcome. Participants should finish this section understanding the main question(s) the study aims to answer and the overall purpose of the research.



STEP 1 — IDENTIFY THE STUDY PHASE/TYPE stated in the protocol (e.g., 'Phase I', 'Phase II', 'Phase III', 'Phase IV', 'pilot study', 'feasibility study').

STEP 2 — SELECT EXACTLY ONE BLOCK from suggested_text and output it as the entire section content. Each option already begins with 'The purpose of this study is to…', so the chosen block IS the required_text fulfilled for that phase — do not output the required_text sentence separately in addition to it. The blocks are mutually exclusive; never combine two phase blocks.
  • Pilot / feasibility study → Option A
  • Phase I safety (standard design) → Option B
  • Phase I dose-escalation / dose-finding → Option C
  • Phase II (efficacy / effects) → Option D
  • Phase III non-placebo-controlled → Option E
  • Phase III placebo-controlled → Option F
  • Phase IV (post-approval) → Option G
  • No matching phase (e.g., registry, non-interventional, or observational study) → do not use any phase block; instead output the required_text sentence alone, filling it with the study objective in plain lay language.

PLACEBO RULE: If a placebo is used anywhere in the study, append the placebo explanation paragraph from suggested_text after the chosen phase block. This applies regardless of which option was selected — not only Option F.
sections.required_text: The purpose of this study is to {{explain the purpose of the study}}.
sections.suggested_text:
NOTE: The blocks below are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE. Choose exactly ONE block that matches the study phase/type. Do not include multiple phase blocks.

<<OPTION A — Pilot / Feasibility Study>>
The purpose of this study, called a pilot study or a feasibility study, is to test the study plan and to find out whether enough participants will join a larger study and accept the study procedures. This type of study involves a small number of participants and so it is not expected to prove safety or effectiveness of {{insert study intervention}}. The results may be used as a guide for larger studies, although there is no guarantee that they will be conducted. Participation in a pilot study does not mean that you will be eligible to participate in a future larger study.

<<OPTION B — Phase I Study (safety, standard design)>>
The purpose of this study is to test the safety of {{describe, e.g., natural health product/drug/device, insert name(s) of product/agent/device}}, to see what effects it has on individuals with {{specify condition}}.

<<OPTION C — Phase I Study (dose-escalation / dose-finding design — use instead of Option B if the protocol describes dose escalation)>>
The purpose of this study is to find the highest dose of {{describe, e.g., natural health product/drug/device, insert name(s) of product/agent/device}}, that can be given without causing very severe side effects. This is done by starting at a dose lower than the one that does not cause side effects in animals.

Participants are given {{insert name(s) of product/agent/device}} and are watched very closely to see what side effects they have and to make sure the side effects are not severe. If the side effects are not severe, then new participants will be given a higher dose of {{insert name(s) of product/agent/device}}. Participants joining this study later on will get higher doses of {{insert name(s) of product/agent/device}} than participants who join earlier.

<Include if dose-escalation continues to maximum tolerated dose:>
This will continue until a dose is found that causes severe but temporary side effects. Doses higher than that will not be given. Your study doctor will tell you at which dose level you will start the study drug.

<<OPTION D — Phase II Study>>
The purpose of this study is to find out what effects {{describe, e.g., natural health product/drug/device, insert name(s) of product/agent/device}}, has on individuals with {{specify condition}}.

<<OPTION E — Phase III Study (non-placebo-controlled comparative)>>
The purpose of this study is to compare the effects of {{describe, e.g., natural health product/drug/device, insert name(s) of product/agent/device}}, to other {{natural health products/drugs/devices}}, which are commonly-used for {{specify condition}}, on individuals with {{specify condition}}.

<<OPTION F — Phase III Placebo-Controlled Study>>
The purpose of this study is to find out {{specify purpose, e.g., whether it is better to receive insert name(s) of product/agent/device}}, or better to receive no additional intervention. To do this, some of the participants in this study will get {{insert name(s) of product/agent/device}} and others will receive a placebo (a substance that looks like the study {{natural health product/drug/device}} but does not have any active or medicinal ingredients).

<If ANY placebo is used — include this explanation regardless of phase:>
A placebo is given in this study to reduce the chances of believing that a disease is getting better because one is receiving a new drug. Really, we don't know if the new drug or no drug {{insert, if applicable, 'with or without the standard drug'}} is better than the other so we are doing this study to try and find that out.

<<OPTION G — Phase IV Study>>
The purpose of this study is to look at an approved intervention to obtain additional information about {{specify purpose e.g., benefits, side effects, etc.}}.

sections.heading: WHAT OTHER CHOICES ARE THERE?
sections.instructions:
Explain the alternative options applicable to the study population, and their important potential benefits and risks.

List applicable treatments available to participants. Should any of the study drug(s)/intervention(s) be available outside of participation in the study, they should be listed here.

Do not include: “This study has been approved by the research ethics committee….” since this may appear to offer a guarantee of safety.
sections.suggested_text:
You do not have to take part in this study in order to receive treatment or care.  Other options (in addition to the standard or usual treatment described above) may include, but are not limited to:<Modify previous line as applicable if there is no other alternative treatment available)>

<List applicable treatments available to participants (examples below may be used as applicable). Should any of the study drug(s)/intervention(s) be available outside of participation in the study, they should be listed here. >
• no therapy at this time
• palliative care or Best Supportive Care (BSC). This type of care helps reduce pain, tiredness, appetite problems and other problems. It does not treat your condition directly, but instead tries to improve how you feel. Best Supportive Care tries to keep you as active and comfortable as possible.
• other research studies may be available if you do not take part in this study

Please talk to your usual doctor or the study doctor about the known benefits and risks of these other options before you decide to take part in this study. Your usual doctor or the study doctor can also discuss with you what will happen if you decide not to undertake any treatment at this time.

<<Suggestion for studies using healthy volunteers>>
You do not have to take part in this study.

sections.heading: HOW MANY PEOPLE WILL TAKE PART IN THIS STUDY?
complexity: Not in protocol - requires manual entry
sections.instructions:
Indicate the total number of participants, where this study is taking place, and how many participants are specifically participating at University Health Network (UHN), inclusive of any UHN sites. Indicate how long the study will take overall and when results are expected to be available. Note: Do not discuss the length of individual participation in the study in this section. This section should indicate the total study length.

UHN-ONLY vs MULTI-SITE wording (resolve the multi-site placeholder in required_text accordingly):
- If this is a UHN-only study: do NOT include the optional location phrase ('from research sites located in' / e.g., Canada / around the world / in North America). Do NOT include a separate closing sentence such as 'It is expected that {{insert number of participants}} will be from UHN.' Instead, condense into the first sentence for flow, e.g.: 'It is anticipated that {{x}} people from UHN will take part in this study.'
- If this is a multi-site study: include a general geographical reference for research site locations (do not specify actual site names; use e.g., 'Canada', 'North America', 'around the world'), and state how many participants are expected from UHN.
sections.required_text:
It is anticipated that about {{insert total number of study participants}} people will take part in this study. {{If research is multi-site, note the locations of other research sites and the number of participants from UHN}}.

This study should take {{total study length in months or years}} to complete and the results should be known in about {{time for anticipated analysis in months or years}}.

sections.heading: WHAT WILL HAPPEN DURING THIS STUDY?
sections.instructions:
If there is more than one study group, describe how participants are placed into study groups. Provide a lay description appropriate to the specific protocol.

RANDOMIZATION: Use the randomized suggested_text block ONLY when the protocol explicitly states that participants are randomized (or assigned by chance). If the study is non-randomized / not randomized, do NOT mention randomization at all. Simply describe how group assignment actually works for this study (or leave this sub-section empty if there is only one group / no group assignment).

DOSE ESCALATION / DOSE COHORTS: If the study uses dose escalation or sequential dose cohorts as part of how participants are assigned to groups, describe how participants are placed into those dose levels or cohorts here. For oncology or cancer dose-escalation studies, explain the dosing approach in general terms without including specific numerical values for dose levels, dose volumes, or escalation cohorts. For non-oncology studies, include key dose information and dosing cohorts when relevant to understanding assignment, while avoiding excessive technical detail.
sections.suggested_text:
<If there is more than one study group: example for randomized studies>

If you decide to participate then you will be "randomized" into one of the groups described below. Randomization means that you are put into a group by chance (like flipping a coin). There is no way to predict which group you will be assigned to. You will have {{explain probability of randomization e.g., an equal/one in three chance of being placed in either/any group}}.  Neither you, the study staff, nor the study doctors can choose what group you will be in.
- Participants in group 1: {{explain what will happen for this group with clear indication of which interventions depart from routine care}}
- Participants in group 2: {{explain what will happen for this group with clear indication of which interventions depart from routine care}}

sections.heading: WHAT WILL HAPPEN DURING THIS STUDY?
sections.instructions: Explain whether participants or others will know which group the participant will be in.
sections.suggested_text:
<For open label, randomized studies>
You will be told which group you are in.

<For single-blind studies>
You will not know which group you are in, but the study doctor and study staff will.

When you finish you participation in the study and would like to know what study group you were in, let the study team know. Please note that you may not be able to get this information until the entire study is completed.

<For double-blind studies>

• Medical History

• Physical Exam

The blood samples will be taken at different visits either before and/or after the study drug is taken. {{Indicate the frequency and the amount of blood (per draw and overall) to be taken and over what interval.}}

• ECG (Electrocardiogram)- An electrocardiogram is a test that measures the electrical activity of the heart. Patches attached by wires to a machine will be put on your chest so that the machine can record the pattern of your heart beats.

• Echo (Echocardiogram) – A test that uses sound waves to create a moving picture of the heart to measure how well your heart is functioning.  The picture is much more detailed that a regular x-ray picture and does not involve any radiation exposure.  An instrument that sends high frequency sound waves will be placed on your ribs near the breastbone directed toward your heart.

• X-ray – {{Specify what part(s) of the body will be scanned}}

• MUGA Scan - A radioactive tracer is injected via IV (inside your vein) which attaches to blood cells.  Then an instrument is used to see inside your heart.

• CT (Computed Tomography) scan - An x-ray machine that makes computerized pictures of the inside of your body

• CT (Computed Tomography) scan with contrast - An x-ray machine that makes computerized pictures of the inside of your body. Prior to the CT scan you will have a dye injected via IV (inside your vein) into your body.

• MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) - Use of magnetic waves to take pictures of the inside of your body.  You will have to lie still in a MRI machine but will be able to speak to someone at all times.

You will have to lie still in a MRI machine but will be able to speak to someone at all times.  Prior to the MRI scan you will have a gadolinium contrast injection via IV (inside your vein).

The PET scan uses a radioactive drug (tracer) to show both, normal and abnormal activities in your body.  The tracer is most often injected into a vein within your hand or arm. {{If otherwise, specify}}. The tracer will then collect into areas of your body that have higher levels of activity, which often pinpoints the location of the disease.

They may give you a drug to help you relax.

sections.heading: WHAT ARE THE RESPONSIBILITIES OF STUDY PARTICIPANTS?
sections.instructions:
Only list responsibilities the participant must personally fulfill during the study. Do not include details of the consent process itself, the statistical analysis plan, or how compensation is administered (compensation details belong in the 'Are Study Participants Paid?' section).

Identify participant responsibilities. Include, add to, or modify the bullets in the suggested text as applicable to the study.

The lead-in sentence 'If you choose to participate in this study, you will be expected to:' is fixed and should always appear before the bullets.

For the last two bullets (study intervention sharing and focus-group confidentiality), include only those that apply to the study modality.
sections.required_text: If you choose to participate in this study, you will be expected to:
sections.suggested_text:
- Tell the study doctor about your current medical conditions
- Tell the study doctor about all prescription and non-prescription medications and supplements, including vitamins and herbals, and check with the study doctor before starting, stopping or changing any of these. This is for your safety as these may interact with the intervention you receive on this study.
- Tell the study doctor if you are thinking about participating in another research study
- Return any unused study medication
- Return any {{specify e.g., diaries or questionnaires}} that you take home to complete
- Tell the study doctor if you become pregnant or father a child while participating on this study
- Avoid drinking/eating {{specify what and for how long}}
- Stop taking {{name}} for {{specify washout period}}
- {{insert name of study intervention}} is for you alone, and must not be shared with others.  {{If applicable, include:}} If someone accidentally takes {{insert name of study intervention, include instructions e.g.,}} they should immediately go to the nearest emergency department.
- Do not discuss with others any information you learn in the focus group.  This includes information about other group members and any opinions or comments that are shared.

sections.heading: HOW LONG WILL PARTICIPANTS BE IN THE STUDY?
sections.instructions:
Specify the duration of intervention, follow-up schedule, and total length of research involvement. Revise as applicable to the research. Note: 'duration of intervention' and 'total length of research involvement' are distinct (e.g., a 6-week treatment plus 2-year follow-up); both should be addressed if they differ.

If intervention length varies by group assignment, ensure this is specified.

FOLLOW-UP VISIT SCHEDULE (second suggested_text paragraph — the 'You will be asked to come back…' block): This paragraph is ONLY for return study-related visits after (or between) intervention periods — when and where the participant is asked to come back to the clinic/hospital for follow-up. Describe the follow-up visit schedule (location and timing of return visits, e.g., clinic/hospital 30 days after the last dose of study drug; then every X months for X years). Do NOT use this paragraph to describe the drug dosing schedule, how often the study drug/intervention is given, or the treatment administration calendar. If the protocol has no return follow-up visits, omit this paragraph.

If there is long-term follow-up as part of the study, include the long-term follow-up paragraph. Define the period of time, describe the purpose of long-term follow-up, and specify the follow-up method and frequency (e.g., in-person visits at the hospital/clinic, or phone calls).

Writing style — apply to all text generated for this section:
• Plain language: use common everyday words and short sentences
• Research framing: use correct research terminology (e.g. "investigational study drug," not "treatment" or "therapy"). Do not imply guaranteed outcomes — state explicitly that benefits are uncertain.
• Participant-centred tone: say "you will be asked to" rather than "you will be expected to". Maintain a neutral, non-coercive, non-persuasive tone throughout.

sections.heading: CAN PARTICIPANTS CHOOSE TO LEAVE THE STUDY?
sections.instructions:
OUTPUT STRUCTURE: The filled template must contain the required_text verbatim as the opening paragraph, followed by the applicable suggested_text blocks resolved for this study.

Insert information on the participant's right to request the withdrawal of data or human biological materials, including any limitations on the feasibility of that withdrawal.

Regulatory guidance (TCPS2): If the study site CONTINUES using the participant's data after they have withdrawn from the study, this must be justified to the REB and explained to the participants. Canadian Guidelines (TCPS2) state that participants should be able to request that data and sample(s) be withdrawn unless withdrawal of data or samples is not possible or is impracticable.

Resolve each conditional in the suggested_text as follows:
- <For clinical trials with regulatory oversight, include the following>: Include if the study is a regulated clinical trial (e.g., Phase I-IV interventional study with Health Canada or FDA oversight) where data recorded prior to withdrawal cannot be removed.
- <OR If the participant can withdraw information collected prior to withdrawal>: Include this paragraph INSTEAD of the regulatory-oversight paragraph if the protocol allows participants to withdraw their data. These two conditionals are mutually exclusive — choose one based on the protocol.
- <Studies involving tissue/blood/body fluids>: Include if the study collects biological samples.

IMPORTANT (regulatory constraint from the UHN template): The participant should NOT be instructed to contact the sponsor directly to withdraw. The participant's identifiable information should remain with the study site, and the participant should only be instructed to contact their study team to withdraw.

IMPORTANT (regulatory constraint from the UHN template): Written withdrawal from participants shall NOT be required. Many participants discontinue verbally or cannot write in English, so no language in this section should imply written withdrawal is required. If the sponsor requires written notification of withdrawal, the study doctor (not the participant) may provide that written notification to the sponsor.
sections.required_text: You can choose to end your participation in this research (called withdrawal) at any time without having to provide a reason.  If you choose to withdraw from the study, you are encouraged to contact the study doctor or study staff.
sections.suggested_text:
You may be asked questions about your experience with the study intervention and to have laboratory tests and physical examinations considered necessary to safely stop your study involvement.

<For clinical trials with regulatory oversight, include the following:>
If you leave the study, information that was recorded before you withdrew will still be used by the researchers in order to answer the research question, but no information will be collected without your permission after you withdraw from the study.

<OR If the participant can withdraw information collected prior to withdrawal:>
If you decide to leave the study, you can ask that the information that was collected about you not be used for the study.  Let the study doctor know if you choose this. Otherwise, information that was recorded before you withdrew will still be used by the researchers for the purposes of the study, but no information will be collected after you withdraw from the study.

<Studies involving tissue/blood/body fluids:>
If you decide to leave the study, you have the right to request withdrawal of your {{insert types of samples as applicable to study – e.g.}} blood, tissue, {{etc.}} Let your study doctor know. Otherwise, samples collected before you withdrew will still be used by the researchers for the purposes of the study, but no information will be collected after you withdraw from the study. The sponsor will keep and use any research results obtained prior to your withdrawal of consent.

sections.heading: CAN PARTICIPATION IN THIS STUDY END EARLY?
sections.instructions:
Identify reasons why participants may be taken off the study. Include ALL bullets from the suggested_text by default. Only omit a bullet if the protocol explicitly contradicts it (e.g., omit the Sponsor bullet only for investigator-initiated studies with no external sponsor; omit the pregnancy bullet only if the protocol explicitly excludes reproductive risk). When in doubt, include the bullet. Do not silently drop bullets because the protocol does not mention them — early termination reasons are standard and apply unless clearly ruled out.

The opening line ('The study doctor may stop your participation...') and the closing line ('If you are removed from this study, the study doctor will discuss the reasons with you.') are fixed/required. The bullets listing reasons, and the optional continuation '...and plans will be made for your continued care outside of the study,' are suggested text and may be edited.

Always include the 'If this happens, it may mean that you would not receive the study intervention for the full period described in this consent form.' sentence after the bullet list when a study intervention is involved.

- The study doctor no longer feels this is the best option for you
- The Sponsor decides to stop the study

- If you plan to or become pregnant

<Optional follow-on after the bullets:>
If this happens, it may mean that you would not receive the study intervention for the full period described in this consent form.

<Optional extension of the closing required sentence — append to the required_text closing if applicable:>

sections.instructions:
YOUR SCOPE FOR THIS SECTION IS NARROW — read carefully.

Your filled_template must contain exactly TWO things and nothing else:
  1. The required_text verbatim (the two opening sentences — do NOT change a word).
  2. The applicable suggested_text with placeholders filled and conditionals resolved:
       - Always include the 'When possible, other medicine will be given...' sentence (the standard side-effects management language).
       - Include the <For studies using non-marketed drugs or other investigational interventions, if applicable> paragraph ONLY if the study uses a non-marketed or investigational drug/device. Omit it for approved standard-of-care drugs.
       - The 911 / emergency room sentence is presented in the source as blue (suggested) text adjacent to the non-marketed-drug paragraph. As a pipeline policy, always include it for participant safety — but be aware this is a UHN-pipeline policy, not a strict source mandate.
       - Fill {{insert name of product/agent/device}} with the study intervention name from the protocol.

DO NOT extract or include any list of side effects or risks here. The detailed risk content belongs exclusively in sub-sections 18.1 (intervention risks) and 18.2 (procedure risks), which are processed separately. Including risk lists here will cause duplication in the final ICF.
sections.required_text:
You may experience side effects from participating in this study.  Some side effects are known and are listed below, but there may be other side effects that are not expected.  You should discuss these with the study doctor.

The study doctor will watch you closely to see if you have side effects.
sections.suggested_text:
When possible, other medicine will be given to you to make side effects less serious and more tolerable. Many side effects go away shortly after the study intervention is stopped, but in some cases side effects can be serious, long-lasting, permanent, or may even cause death.

<For studies using non-marketed drugs or other investigational interventions if applicable:>
If you experience a side effect that requires treatment between regular clinic/hospital visits, it is important that you make every effort to return to the clinic/hospital where {{insert name of product/agent/device}} was given. Because {{insert name of product/agent/device}} is experimental and is only used in clinics/hospitals involved in research studies, any side effects may be best treated by these clinics/hospitals.

If you experience a serious side effect and need immediate treatment and are unable to return to the clinic/hospital, please call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room. Then the study doctor should be contacted as soon as possible.

sections.heading: WHAT ARE THE RISKS OR HARMS OF PARTICIPATING IN THIS STUDY?
sections.instructions:
Construct the risk list for the experimental intervention from the protocol and Investigator Brochure/Product Monograph, then substitute it into the required_text placeholder {{list of side effects}}.

Nature of risks to include: Describe all reasonably foreseeable risks, harms, or discomforts. Include both physical and psychological/emotional risks as applicable to the research. A rare but serious finding from previous studies (e.g., death, severe pneumonitis, acute renal failure, etc.) should be placed at the top of the list of side effects or should be bolded.

Language: Include lay language explanation of any side effects.

Categorization: When detailed information about the side effect profile for the intervention is known, categorize risks by frequency. Examples of these categories are provided in the suggested_text — other categorizations may be used depending on the presentation of risks in the Investigator Brochure/Product Monograph.

Information to provide: address frequency, severity, and long-term impact or reversibility. When applicable, specific symptoms for serious side effects of which the participant should be aware (e.g., in order to seek immediate medical assistance) should be included.

It is not necessary to describe the risks associated with tests or procedures with which the participant population would already be familiar.

Explain the significance of a side effect if not obvious.

Include risk of receiving placebo / delayed surgery / delayed or withdrawn standard of care treatment, if applicable.

Address psychological risks such as anxiety, distress, embarrassment, or feelings of sadness that may arise from questionnaires and interviews about sensitive issues (e.g., mental health, sexuality).

Separate side effects of each drug and procedure as appropriate.

Consider using bullets (or sub-sections, as appropriate) for each of the side effects.

List each side effect of a drug/procedure only once, provide a full description of the side effect under the same bullet, and indicate its severity, if applicable.

For Phase II and Phase III studies where previous safety data are available, the REB expects that the upper range of frequency be provided. A 'greater than 10/20%' response is generally not acceptable without justification. The REB evaluates the presentation of the side effects on a 'study-by-study' basis, severity of the side effects, and their relevance to the study population.

Serious side effects that have not been clearly linked to the study drug should also be included.

Possible treatment options of side effects should NOT be discussed in the consent form — should a side effect occur, it would be treated according to the individual's situation and might differ from the options listed. Moreover, listing treatment options may leave the impression that those treatments are part of the study intervention, while they are not.

Should an extensive list of side effects per drug be identified, to improve readability and increase the participant's comprehension, consider grouping side effects in a meaningful way for participants (e.g., per system, per syndrome). Presenting an extensive list of side effects in alphabetical order is NOT acceptable.

Should a standard-of-care drug(s)/treatment be administered as part of the study intervention, the most common and most severe side effects from that standard-of-care intervention should be presented.

Should an experimental combination of the drugs be administered during the study, potential side effects should be listed for each of the drugs individually. Then, under the combination, only side effects not listed for either of the drugs and/or side effects that have been seen at an increased frequency compared to either of the drugs administered alone should be presented. After per-drug side effects are presented, the consent form should have language indicating that 'any of these side effects may occur with the combination of the drugs, some of them could be more severe, may occur at an increased frequency, and new side effects, not seen with either of the drugs, may happen.'

If a combination has been studied extensively (e.g., at the sponsor's request to have all side effects listed for the combination), in addition to the above, an appendix to the consent form presenting a comprehensive list of the side effects of the combination could be considered.

If more data on a combination than on the study drugs individually are available, the side effects could be listed for the combination first, followed by the presentation of the side effects for each drug individually presenting only side effects not listed for the combination and/or side effects that have been seen at the increased frequency with either of the drugs administered alone.

Writing style — apply to all text generated for this section:
• Plain language: use common everyday words and short sentences. Spell out any abbreviation or acronym on first use.
• Research framing: use correct research terminology (e.g. "investigational study drug," not "treatment" or "therapy"). Do not imply guaranteed outcomes — state explicitly that benefits are uncertain.
• Participant-centred tone: say "you will be asked to" rather than "you will be expected to". Maintain a neutral, non-coercive, non-persuasive tone throughout.

sections.heading: WHAT ARE THE REPRODUCTIVE RISKS?
complexity: Not in protocol - requires manual entry
sections.instructions:
If the agent(s) used in the study present a real or potential risk of fetal or reproductive harm, this must be described.  Generic wording for unknown risk is included in the suggested_text template.

If there are known interactions or contraindications with specific contraceptive methods, those should be included as additional text by the form author (no template language is provided for this — write it inline as applicable to the protocol).

For the turquoise placeholder {{you/they}} in the effects paragraph, pick the appropriate pronoun based on whether the participant themself or their partner could become pregnant.

The 'sperm mutation / teratogenic risk' conditional applies specifically when the intervention may cause sperm mutation or teratogenic effects. The 'unable to have children in the future' paragraph that follows is STANDALONE (applies broadly to studies whose intervention may affect fertility, e.g. chemotherapy, hormonal treatments) — include it independently of the sperm-mutation conditional based on whether infertility risk applies.

The 'For trials with pregnancy reporting' conditional applies when the protocol requires pregnancy follow-up. Include all three paragraphs under this conditional as a group.

Regulatory/policy guidance (from the UHN template): Some sponsors would like to follow pregnancy for safety reporting. A person should not be asked to give consent to collect information about a future uncertain event at the time of consenting for the study since the circumstances surrounding the decisions could be different at that time. This is a decision that they and, possibly, their partner would want to make at that time. Also, once they become pregnant, they are withdrawn from the study and all rights to collect information are lost. Therefore, pregnant participants must be consented to be followed. They should be re-consented using a separate consent form to give permission for their pregnancy to be followed.
